claims.source: Retinal vascular diseases can lead to vision loss.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claims.claim: Abnormalities in retinal vasculature morphology and physiology serve as important biomarkers for various cerebral and systemic diseases.
claims.source: Abnormalities in retinal vasculature morphology and physiology serve as important biomarkers for various cerebral and systemic diseases (Patton et al., 2005; Frost et al., 2013; Ikram et al., 2013; Liew et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: After AO correction, a 2–10× enhancement in signal was observed for retinal vessels.
claims.source: After AO correction, we observed a 2–10× enhancement in signal (Figure 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: AO's impact on signal of smaller capillaries (6–10× improvement) was more substantial than on larger vessels (2–3× improvement).
claims.source: Comparing the line signal profiles (along the orange dashed lines, Figure 2A and B), we found that AO improved signal for all vessels while its impact on signal of smaller capillaries (Figure 2C, black asterisks; 6–10× improvement) was more substantial than on larger vessels (Figure 2C, black circles; 2–3× improvement).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Most capillaries could be resolved in 3D without AO by the optimized 2PFM, albeit at reduced contrast and resolution.
claims.source: Despite the substantial signal improvements enabled by AO, we found that most capillaries, due to their size and sparse distribution in space, could be resolved in 3D without AO by our optimized 2PFM, albeit at reduced contrast and resolution (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: A properly designed 2PFM is capable of acquiring retinal angiograms at the level of individual capillaries.
claims.source: Our results indicate that a properly designed 2PFM is capable of acquiring retinal angiograms at the level of individual capillaries.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 2.

claims.claim: AO performed at the superficial plexus was beneficial for imaging deeper layers.
claims.source: We found that AO performed at the superficial plexus was beneficial for imaging deeper layers, with the correction at superficial depth improving signal, resolution, and contrast of deeper vasculature (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: Most aberrations of the mouse eye arose from cornea and crystalline lens, instead of retina.
claims.source: This result indicated that most aberrations of the mouse eye arose from cornea and crystalline lens, instead of retina.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that AO at superficial depth benefits deeper imaging.

claims.claim: The crystalline lens of the mouse eye has a gradient refractive index distribution.
claims.source: Because the crystalline lens of the mouse eye has a gradient refractive index distribution (Campbell and Hughes, 1981; Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), ocular aberrations should also be field dependent (Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: Ocular aberrations should be field dependent.
claims.source: Because the crystalline lens of the mouse eye has a gradient refractive index distribution (Campbell and Hughes, 1981; Remtulla and Hallett, 1985), ocular aberrations should also be field dependent (Wang and Ji, 2012; Wang and Ji, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations and reasoning.

claims.claim: Signal improvement ('AO/No AO' pixel ratio ≥1) was found within a radius of ~216 µm when AO was performed at the FOV center.
claims.source: We found signal improvement ('AO/No AO' pixel ratio ≥1) within a radius of ~216 µm when AO was performed at the FOV center of this mouse (Figure 2F, [1]).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: For off-center locations, the radius of signal improvement was slightly smaller than for center locations.
claims.source: For off-center locations, this radius was slightly smaller (Figure 2F, [2] and [3]).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The mouse retina consists of multiple layers of neurons with different cell types and distinct physiological properties.
claims.source: The mouse retina consists of multiple layers of neurons with different cell types and distinct physiological properties.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about retinal anatomy.

claims.claim: In the early stage of retinal diseases, abnormal morphology and function are usually confined to specific cell types within a single layer.
claims.source: In the early stage of retinal diseases, abnormal morphology and function are usually confined to specific cell types within a single layer (Hoon et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citation.

claims.claim: A single AO correction substantially improved signal and resolution for densely fluorescent Thy1-YFP-16 mouse retina.
claims.source: A single AO correction acquired by scanning a 19×19 µm2 area centered on the red asterisk in (Figure 3A) substantially improved signal and resolution (Figure 3A and B; Figure 3—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: AO recovered higher spatial frequency information, thus improving both lateral and axial resolution.
claims.source: 2D Fourier transforms of these retinal images indicated that AO recovered higher spatial frequency information (i.e. farther away from the center of Figure 3C and D) thus improved both lateral and axial resolution.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The resolution enhancement was especially striking along the axial direction, allowing retinal layers to be more clearly differentiated.
claims.source: The resolution enhancement was especially striking along the axial direction, allowing retinal layers to be more clearly differentiated by better resolving neurons at different depths (Figure 3A and B, XZ images).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Improvement in axial resolution minimizes neuropil contamination and ensures accurate characterization of the functional properties of neurons.
claims.source: This improvement in axial resolution is especially important for functional imaging, because it minimizes neuropil contamination and ensures accurate characterization of the functional properties of neurons (Ji et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014a; Sun et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: AO was necessary for 3D cellular resolution imaging of retinal neurons in vivo.
claims.source: Therefore, AO was necessary for 3D cellular resolution imaging of retinal neurons in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The optimized 2PFM design and mouse preparation allowed the identification of individual neurons without AO in lateral image planes, albeit at lower signal and poorer resolution than with AO.
claims.source: In the lateral image planes, our optimized 2PFM design and mouse preparation allowed the identification of individual neurons without AO, albeit at lower signal and poorer resolution than those achieved with AO, for inner nuclear layer, inner plexiform layer, and ganglion cell layer (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Subcellular processes could not be clearly visualized without aberration correction.
claims.source: In contrast, subcellular processes could not be clearly visualized without aberration correction (e.g. processes in the inner plexiform layer, Figure 3E, white boxes in the middle column; more examples in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The Thy1-YFP-16 mouse eye exhibited field-dependent aberrations.
claims.source: Similar to our vascular imaging results, the Thy1-YFP-16 mouse eye exhibited field-dependent aberrations.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: For the Thy1-YFP-16 mouse, the effective area of AO performed at the FOV center was estimated to have a radius of ~185 µm.
claims.source: For the Thy1-YFP-16 mouse, the effective area of AO performed at the FOV center was estimated from the 'AO/No AO' ratio map (Figure 3G) to have a radius of ~185 µm (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claims.claim: Correcting aberrations from smaller areas provided greater local signal improvement but exhibited faster decay in signal improvement over distance.
claims.source: Quantifying and comparing AO effectiveness by their 'AO/No AO' pixel ratio maps (Figure 4A), we found that correcting aberrations from smaller areas provided greater local signal improvement but exhibited faster decay in signal improvement over distance (Figure 4B, i and ii).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Correcting aberrations from a larger area reduced signal improvement in the center but enlarged the overall area within which signal was enhanced.
claims.source: In contrast, correcting aberrations from a larger area reduced signal improvement in the center of the area but enlarged the overall area within which signal was enhanced, which now extended over the entire imaging FOV (Figure 4B, iii and iv).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: A localized wavefront measurement is required for diffraction-limited imaging of fine structures within a small FOV.
claims.source: Our results suggest that for diffraction-limited imaging of fine structures within a small FOV, a localized wavefront measurement is required, whereas a global wavefront measurement is preferable for 3D cellular resolution imaging over large FOVs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 4.

claims.claim: A global wavefront measurement is preferable for 3D cellular resolution imaging over large FOVs.
claims.source: Our results suggest that for diffraction-limited imaging of fine structures within a small FOV, a localized wavefront measurement is required, whereas a global wavefront measurement is preferable for 3D cellular resolution imaging over large FOVs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Retinal angiomatous proliferation (RAP) is a subtype of age-related macular degeneration.
claims.source: Retinal angiomatous proliferation (RAP), a subtype of age-related macular degeneration, is characterized by capillary proliferation that originates from the sensory retina and extends into the subretinal space (Yannuzzi et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citation.

claims.claim: RAP is characterized by capillary proliferation that originates from the sensory retina and extends into the subretinal space.
claims.source: Retinal angiomatous proliferation (RAP), a subtype of age-related macular degeneration, is characterized by capillary proliferation that originates from the sensory retina and extends into the subretinal space (Yannuzzi et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citation.

claims.claim: The VLDLR-KO mouse model replicates the characteristic phenotypes of human RAP.
claims.source: Replicating the characteristic phenotypes of human RAP, a transgenic mouse model, the very low-density lipoprotein receptor knockout (VLDLR-KO) mouse, has been employed to study the underlying mechanism of RAP.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the mouse model.

claims.claim: In the VLDLR-KO model, the gene encoding VLDLR is knocked out, leading to overgrown intraretinal vasculature and subretinal neovascularization.
claims.source: In this model, the gene encoding VLDLR, which mediates anti-angiogenic signaling in retinal vasculature, is knocked out, leading to overgrown intraretinal vasculature and subretinal neovascularization (Heckenlively et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: The VLDLR-KO model of proliferative vascular retinopathy has extensive focal vascular leakage.
claims.source: In addition, fluorescein angiography revealed that the VLDLR-KO model of proliferative vascular retinopathy has extensive focal vascular leakage (Heckenlively et al., 2003; Hu et al., 2008; Li, 2007; Xia et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: The lack of sufficient spatial resolution and optical sectioning capability makes it challenging for fluorescence angiography to identify the 3D location and characterize the structure of vascular lesions in vivo.
claims.source: However, the lack of sufficient spatial resolution and optical sectioning capability makes it challenging for fluorescence angiography to identify the 3D location and characterize the structure of the vascular lesions in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of fluorescence angiography.

claims.claim: In the VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP retina, images acquired with AO revealed a disruption in the capillary endothelium where endothelial cells lined the walls of a short capillary branch but not its end face, leading to a ring-like structure.
claims.source: Interestingly, in the VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP retina, images acquired with AO revealed a disruption in the capillary endothelium labeled by GFP, where the endothelial cells lined the walls of a short capillary branch but not its end face, leading to a ring-like structure (Figure 5A and C, yellow asterisks, insets i-ii; Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claims.claim: Ring-like structures were not observed in the WT/Sca1-GFP retina.
claims.source: Such ring-like structures were not observed in the WT/Sca1-GFP retina (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Capillaries in the wildtype control had endothelial cells fully enclosing both the walls and the ends of capillary branches.
claims.source: Whereas similarly structured capillary disruptions were observed in the VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP retina, consistent with the in vivo investigation, capillaries in the wildtype control had endothelial cells fully enclosing both the walls and the ends of capillary branches (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D; Figure 5—video 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from ex vivo experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D.

claims.claim: Dye leakage was observed around the lesion site immediately after FITC injection in the VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP mouse retina.
claims.source: Immediately after dye injection, we observed dye leakage around the lesion site (Figure 5D, orange dashed area).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Neither capillary disruptions nor dye leakage were observed in the healthy WT/Sca1-GFP mouse retina after FITC injection.
claims.source: A control experiment was carried out by introducing FITC into the healthy WT/Sca1-GFP mouse retina retro-orbitally, where neither capillary disruptions nor dye leakage were observed (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: EB persistently stained retinal tissue and the stained volume expanded over 3 days of consecutive imaging in the VLDLR-KO retina.
claims.source: Similar to the experiments with FITC, we observed leakage in the knockout mouse retina, with EB persistently staining retinal tissue and the stained volume expanding over 3 days of consecutive imaging (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Capillary lesions were observed in the EB-stained volume, suggesting a spatial correlation between dye leakage and capillary abnormalities.
claims.source: We observed capillary lesions (Figure 5F, insets) in the stained volume, suggesting a spatial correlation between dye leakage and capillary abnormalities.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: GFP-positive cells within the dye-stained retinal volume were observed on the third day that were absent in previous 2 days.
claims.source: Moreover, on the third day, we observed GFP-positive cells within the dye-stained retinal volume that were absent in previous 2 days (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The morphology of the GFP-positive cells resembled that of activated microglia.
claims.source: The morphology of these cells resembled that of activated microglia (Joseph et al., 2021; Ozaki et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: The leakage of EB triggered local immune response and recruited ocular immune cells to the impacted area.
claims.source: We speculated that the leakage of EB triggered local immune response and recruited ocular immune cells to the impacted area.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of GFP-positive cells.

claims.claim: AO was essential for 2PFM to achieve high-resolution identification and characterization of microvasculature lesions in vivo.
claims.source: Here, AO was essential for 2PFM to achieve high-resolution identification and characterization of microvasculature lesions in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 5.

claims.claim: RGCs in the rd1 mouse become hyperactive after photoreceptor death caused by a mutation in the Pde6b gene.
claims.source: RGCs in the rd1 mouse, the oldest and most widely studied animal model of retinal degeneration (Chang et al., 2002), become hyperactive after photoreceptor death caused by a mutation in the Pde6b gene (Sekirnjak et al., 2011; Telias et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: RGC hyperactivity masks light-evoked signals initiated by surviving photoreceptors and impedes remaining light-elicited behaviors.
claims.source: Recent studies have suggested that RGC hyperactivity masks light-evoked signals initiated by surviving photoreceptors and impedes remaining light-elicited behaviors (Telias et al., 2019; Telias et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: RGC hyperactivity has been only studied ex vivo on dissected retinas.
claims.source: However, RGC hyperactivity has been only studied ex vivo on dissected retinas (Telias et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2021), preventing longitudinal evaluation of degeneration progression and therapeutic approaches.
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: RGC hyperactivity measured ex vivo was correlated with a heightened ΔF/F of the GCaMP6s-expressing soma.
claims.source: In terms of calcium signaling (quantified as calcium response magnitude ΔF/F, with F being baseline brightness and ΔF being the difference from baseline brightness), hyperactivity measured ex vivo was correlated with a heightened ΔF/F of the GCaMP6s-expressing soma.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: A temporally varying firing rate led to transient fluctuations in calcium signal.
claims.source: A temporally varying firing rate led to transient fluctuations in its calcium signal (ROI 1, Figure 6A), whereas a sustained high firing rate led to heightened fluorescence brightness without obvious transients (ROI 2, Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: A sustained high firing rate led to heightened fluorescence brightness without obvious transients.
claims.source: A temporally varying firing rate led to transient fluctuations in its calcium signal (ROI 1, Figure 6A), whereas a sustained high firing rate led to heightened fluorescence brightness without obvious transients (ROI 2, Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: After ~20 seconds of 2% Lidocaine bath perfusion, spontaneous spiking from the RGC was largely suppressed with a ΔF/F close to 0.
claims.source: After ~20 seconds of 2% Lidocaine bath perfusion, spontaneous spiking from the RGC was largely suppressed with a ΔF/F close to 0.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: After ACSF washout, RGC hyperactivity partially recovered, which was associated with an increase of ΔF/F magnitude.
claims.source: After artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) washout, RGC hyperactivity partially recovered, which was associated with an increase of ΔF/F magnitude.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The observed time course and suppressive effect of Lidocaine application on RGC hyperactivity were consistent with ex vivo multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings.
claims.source: The observed time course and suppressive effect of Lidocaine application on RGC hyperactivity were consistent with ex vivo multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: AO increased RGC brightness by on average 4× in the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse.
claims.source: Through the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse eye, AO increased RGC brightness by on average 4× and enabled high-resolution visualization of both RGC somata and their processes (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: AO enabled high-resolution visualization of both RGC somata and their processes in the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse.
claims.source: Through the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse eye, AO increased RGC brightness by on average 4× and enabled high-resolution visualization of both RGC somata and their processes (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The RGCs in the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse had dimmer fluorescence than the other lines investigated.
claims.source: The signal increase enabled by AO was particularly important for the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse, because the RGCs here had dimmer fluorescence than the other lines that we investigated.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on comparison across different mouse lines.

claims.claim: Correcting the eye-induced aberration was essential for visualization and high-fidelity functional investigations of RGCs at cellular resolution in vivo in the rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s mouse.
claims.source: For these RGCs, correcting the eye-induced aberration was essential for their visualization and high-fidelity functional investigations at cellular resolution in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Before injecting Lidocaine, slow fluctuations in the brightness of GCaMP6s-expressing RGCs were observed.
claims.source: Before injecting Lidocaine, we observed slow fluctuations in the brightness of GCaMP6s-expressing RGCs (Figure 6D, i), similar to the slow dynamic events in RGC calcium traces measured ex vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: One minute after retro-orbital injection of Lidocaine, hyperactivities from RGCs were substantially inhibited for an hour as indicated by the reduction of RGC GCaMP6s fluorescence brightness.
claims.source: One minute after retro-orbital injection of Lidocaine into the non-imaged eye, hyperactivities from these cells were substantially inhibited for an hour as indicated by the reduction of RGC GCaMP6s fluorescence brightness (Figure 6D, ii and iii).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Imaging the same RGCs 60 min after Lidocaine injection, partial recovery of RGC brightness was detected.
claims.source: Imaging the same RGCs 60 min after injection (Figure 6D, iv), we detected partial recovery of RGC brightness, consistent with our ex vivo recordings after washing out.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: This work demonstrated the first in vivo visualization of putative retinal synaptic structures.
claims.source: By optimizing optical design and sample preparation and using direct wavefront sensing AO to correct mouse eye aberrations, we demonstrated here the first in vivo visualization of putative retinal synaptic structures
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from Figure 1C.

claims.claim: This work demonstrated the first in vivo identification of capillary lesions with sub-capillary details.
claims.source: By optimizing optical design and sample preparation and using direct wavefront sensing AO to correct mouse eye aberrations, we demonstrated here the first in vivo visualization of putative retinal synaptic structures, the first in vivo identification of capillary lesions with sub-capillary details
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from Figure 5.

claims.claim: This work demonstrated the first in vivo detection of RGC hyperactivity and its suppression by pharmacological reagents.
claims.source: By optimizing optical design and sample preparation and using direct wavefront sensing AO to correct mouse eye aberrations, we demonstrated here the first in vivo visualization of putative retinal synaptic structures, the first in vivo identification of capillary lesions with sub-capillary details, and the first in vivo detection of RGC hyperactivity and its suppression by pharmacological reagents.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from Figure 6.

claims.claim: Using the mouse eye's optics itself to focus excitation light and collect fluorescence emission is preferable to using a standard objective lens for in vivo mouse retinal imaging.
claims.source: For this reason, to achieve the best image quality and the largest FOV size, using mouse eye itself as the focusing element as implemented here is preferable.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from reasoning about optical aberrations.

claims.claim: For the multiple mouse strains investigated, ocular aberrations were typically within the range of 3~5 µm peak-to-valley and 0.4~0.8 µm rms.
claims.source: For the multiple mouse strains investigated here (i.e. wild-type (C57BL/6), Thy1-GFP line M, Thy1-YFP-16, VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP, WT/Sca1-GFP, and rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s), we found that their ocular aberrations were typically within the range of 3~5 µm peak-to-valley (P-V; after removing tip, tilt, and defocus) and 0.4~0.8 µm rms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) without notable differences in severity across strains.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: There were no notable differences in severity of ocular aberrations across the mouse strains investigated.
claims.source: For the multiple mouse strains investigated here (i.e. wild-type (C57BL/6), Thy1-GFP line M, Thy1-YFP-16, VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP, WT/Sca1-GFP, and rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s), we found that their ocular aberrations were typically within the range of 3~5 µm peak-to-valley (P-V; after removing tip, tilt, and defocus) and 0.4~0.8 µm rms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) without notable differences in severity across strains.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: With the carefully designed microscope and system aberration correction procedure, capillary visualization, 2D single-cell resolution, and retinal layer differentiation were achieved by only correcting system aberrations.
claims.source: In contrast, with our carefully designed microscope and system aberration correction procedure, we achieved capillary visualization, 2D single-cell resolution, and retinal layer differentiation by only correcting system aberrations ('No AO' in our case).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: A well-engineered 2PFM should be sufficient for in vivo retinal imaging applications requiring only capillary and 2D cellular resolution.
claims.source: Given that our system aberrations were much smaller than mouse ocular aberrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), our study indicated that a well-engineered 2PFM like ours should be sufficient for in vivo retinal imaging applications requiring only capillary and 2D cellular resolution.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The specially designed 0-diopter contact lens encircled with a supportive flat base was essential for high-quality imaging by 2PFM both without and with AO.

claims.claim: The application of the contact lens smoothed corneal defects and reduced wavefront error of the anterior segment of the eye.

claims.claim: The supportive flat base encircling the optical zone of the contact lens and the gel completely separated the eye surface from air and prevented cataract formation.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the function of the contact lens design, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The contact lens and gel enabled high-quality SH images and accurate corrective wavefronts to be acquired throughout the experiment.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: SLO has been combined with calcium imaging to characterize the dynamic functional changes of RGCs in disease models.
claims.source: SLO has been combined with calcium imaging to characterize the dynamic functional changes of RGCs in disease models (Yin et al., 2013; Cheong et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: The visible excitation light utilized in SLO activates photoreceptors, requiring additional considerations in experimental designs.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of SLO.

claims.claim: Without correcting the wavefront distortion introduced by the ocular tissue, the resolution of SLO is limited to cellular level.

claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of SLO without AO.

claims.claim: The NIR excitation light utilized in 2PFM minimizes photoreceptor activation.

claims.claim: Aberration correction by AO enables subcellular resolution to be achieved in vivo with 2PFM.
claims.source: In contrast, the NIR excitation light utilized in 2PFM minimizes photoreceptor activation; aberration correction by AO also enables subcellular resolution to be achieved in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of AO-2PFM, supported by the study's findings.

claims.claim: Investigation of retinal vascular abnormalities in human applications are limited to capillary resolution.
claims.source: Importantly, to probe microscopic early-stage pathologies, high spatial resolution is needed. In human applications, investigation of retinal vascular abnormalities are limited to capillary resolution (Jia et al., 2015; Hormel et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sub-capillary morphology and dynamics of the mouse retina were recently observed by light-sheet microscopy with ex vivo preparations.
claims.source: Sub-capillary morphology and dynamics of the mouse retina were recently observed by light-sheet microscopy, however with ex vivo preparations (Prahst et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a statement supported by citation.

claims.claim: Sub-capillary features had not been observed in the living mouse eye previously.
claims.source: To our knowledge, sub-capillary features had not been observed in the living mouse eye previously.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.

claims.claim: AO enabled identification of capillary lesions as capillary endothelium disruptions that were associated with dye leakage in two-photon fluorescence angiograms.
claims.source: Recovering diffraction-limited resolution, AO enabled us to identify capillary lesions as capillary endothelium disruptions that were associated with dye leakage in two-photon fluorescence angiograms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 5.

claims.claim: The repeatable and reliable AO performance allowed tracking of the same retinal region over multiple days and imaging of cell migration at subcellular resolution.
claims.source: Moreover, the repeatable and reliable AO performance allowed us to track the same retinal region over multiple days and image cell migration at subcellular resolution.

results.result: Adaptive optics (AO) is essential for achieving subcellular and three-dimensional cellular resolution in the mouse retina in vivo. AO correction led to 8.6-10.6× signal increases, enabled visualization of putative synaptic structures for the first time, and achieved lateral resolution of ~0.8 µm and axial resolution of 6.7 µm, approaching theoretical diffraction limits.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C32, C33, C48-C53, C73, and C115 collectively demonstrate that AO is essential for high-resolution retinal imaging. The quantitative improvements in signal (8.6-10.6×), resolution measurements (~0.8 µm lateral, 6.7 µm axial), and first-time visualization of synaptic structures (C51) provide strong converging evidence from Figures 1 and 3.

results.result: A well-engineered 2PFM with optimized sample preparation can achieve 2D cellular resolution and capillary visualization without AO correction, though at reduced contrast and resolution compared to AO-corrected imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C59, C60, C74, C121, and C122 demonstrate that proper system design enables 2D cellular imaging without AO. The experimental data in Figures 2 and 3 show that capillaries and individual neurons can be resolved in lateral planes without AO, though with reduced quality. This finding is important for clarifying discrepancies in the literature (C25-C30).

results.result: AO-2PFM enabled the first in vivo identification of capillary lesions with sub-capillary details in the VLDLR-KO mouse model of proliferative vascular retinopathy. Ring-like capillary endothelium disruptions were identified and spatially correlated with dye leakage.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C34, C88, C89, C91-C94, C98, C116, and C136 demonstrate novel sub-capillary resolution imaging in vivo. The identification of ring-like endothelium disruptions (C88) absent in controls (C89), their correlation with dye leakage (C91, C93, C94), and confirmation by ex vivo imaging (C90) provide strong converging evidence from Figure 5.

results.result: AO-2PFM enabled high-fidelity in vivo detection of RGC hyperactivity in the rd1 retinal degeneration model and demonstrated that Lidocaine effectively suppresses this hyperactivity. AO increased RGC brightness by 4× and was essential for visualization in this dim fluorescence model.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C36, C102-C106, C108, C109, C111, C113, C114, C117, and C140 demonstrate the application of AO-2PFM to pharmacology. The correlation between calcium signals and hyperactivity (C102-C104), Lidocaine suppression (C105, C113), and partial recovery (C106, C114) are well-documented in Figure 6. The 4× signal increase from AO (C108) was essential for this dim model (C111).

results.result: AO-2PFM enabled longitudinal tracking of cell migration in vivo in the VLDLR-KO model. GFP-positive cells resembling activated microglia were observed in dye-stained regions on day 3, suggesting immune response to vascular leakage.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C95, C96, C97, and C137 describe cell migration observations. While the appearance of GFP-positive cells (C95) and their morphological resemblance to microglia (C96) are documented in Figure 5G, the interpretation as immune response (C97) is explicitly stated as speculation. The cell identity is not definitively confirmed, and the causal relationship between leakage and cell recruitment requires further validation.

results.result: AO correction provided 2-10× signal enhancement for retinal vessels, with greater impact on smaller capillaries (6-10×) than larger vessels (2-3×). AO performed at the superficial plexus improved imaging of deeper layers, indicating that most aberrations arise from the cornea and crystalline lens rather than the retina.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C58, C61, and C62 are well-supported by quantitative data in Figure 2. The differential impact on vessel size (C58) and depth-independent benefit (C61) logically support the inference that aberrations originate primarily from anterior optics (C62). This is consistent with the known optical properties of the mouse eye.

results.result: Mouse ocular aberrations are field-dependent, with AO correction effective within a radius of ~185-216 µm from the wavefront sensing location. Localized wavefront measurements provide greater local improvement but faster spatial decay, while global measurements enable 3D cellular resolution over larger FOVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C66, C76-C81 characterize the spatial extent and optimization of AO correction. The quantitative measurements of effective radii (C65, C77) and the trade-off between local and global corrections (C78, C79) are well-documented in Figures 2F, 3G-H, and 4. The strategic recommendations (C80, C81) logically follow from the experimental observations.

results.result: AO substantially improved signal and resolution in densely fluorescent Thy1-YFP-16 retina, with particularly striking enhancement in axial resolution that enables better differentiation of retinal layers and minimizes neuropil contamination for functional imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 describe AO improvements in the Thy1-YFP-16 model. The substantial signal and resolution improvements (C69), recovery of higher spatial frequencies (C70), and enhanced axial resolution (C71) are demonstrated in Figure 3A-D. The importance for functional imaging (C72) is supported by citations and logical reasoning about neuropil contamination.

results.result: A custom-designed 0-diopter contact lens with eye gel reduced aberrations, prevented cataract formation, and enabled high-quality wavefront sensing and imaging for hours. The contact lens and gel separated the eye surface from air and improved imaging quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46, C123, C125, and C126 describe the sample preparation optimization. The benefits of the contact lens are demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, showing improved imaging and wavefront sensing quality. The mechanism (C125) is supported by citation (C124) and the experimental observations are consistent with preventing corneal drying.

results.result: Ocular aberrations across multiple mouse strains (C57BL/6, Thy1-GFP line M, Thy1-YFP-16, VLDLR-KO/Sca1-GFP, WT/Sca1-GFP, rd1-Thy1-GCaMP6s) were typically 3-5 µm peak-to-valley and 0.4-0.8 µm rms, with no notable differences in severity across strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C119 and C120 provide quantitative characterization of aberrations across six mouse strains. The data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 support these measurements. This finding is important for resolving discrepancies in the literature (C25-C30) and establishing that aberration magnitude is consistent across commonly used strains.

results.result: The electrically tunable lens (ETL) introduced minimal aberrations at different control currents, with axial focal shift varying linearly with ETL current and field-of-view size remaining mostly constant.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 characterize the ETL performance. The findings are documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and demonstrate that the ETL does not introduce significant additional aberrations. This is important for validating the optical design and ensuring that observed aberrations are primarily from the mouse eye.

results.result: Subcellular processes could not be clearly visualized without aberration correction in the Thy1-YFP-16 mouse retina.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 is directly supported by Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, showing that processes in the inner plexiform layer require AO for clear visualization. This complements the finding that 2D cellular resolution is achievable without AO (C74) but subcellular features require AO correction.

results.result: The time course and suppressive effect of Lidocaine on RGC hyperactivity observed in calcium imaging were consistent with ex vivo multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 validates the calcium imaging approach by comparing it to electrophysiology. The consistency between methods shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B strengthens confidence in using calcium signals as a readout for RGC hyperactivity. This cross-validation is important for establishing the method's reliability.

results.result: The retina is the only neural tissue whose physiology and pathology can be non-invasively probed by optical microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C12 state established knowledge about retinal accessibility. While this is a well-accepted fact in the field, the claim is somewhat overstated as other neural tissues can be imaged through thinned skull or optical windows, though these are more invasive. The claim is essentially correct in the context of completely non-invasive imaging through natural optics.

results.result: Using the mouse eye's optics itself to focus excitation light is preferable to using a standard objective lens for in vivo mouse retinal imaging, and a well-engineered 2PFM should be sufficient for applications requiring only capillary and 2D cellular resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C118 and C122 present design recommendations based on the study's findings. The preference for using the eye's optics (C118) is logically supported by reasoning about aberrations from the crystalline lens. The sufficiency of well-engineered 2PFM for certain applications (C122) is supported by the experimental results showing 2D cellular resolution without AO (C31, C121).
